questions.question: Which of these can only be written with a `type` alias, not an `interface`?
options: A shape that a class implements
questions.explanation: Interfaces describe object shapes. Unions, tuples, primitives and other non-object types can only be named with type.

questions.question: What happens when you declare `interface AppConfig` twice in the same scope with different properties?
options: The second declaration replaces the first
Only the first declaration is used
The declarations merge into one interface with all properties
questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging. Declaring the same type alias twice is a Duplicate identifier error.

questions.question: Given `interface Base { id: string }`, what is the effect of `type ChildT = Base & { id: number }`?
options: No error at the declaration, but id becomes an impossible type (never), so no value can satisfy it
An immediate error saying ChildT incorrectly extends Base
The later id: number overrides the earlier one
questions.explanation: Intersections combine property types with &, so id is string & number, which is never. extends would report the conflict immediately instead.

questions.question: Why is declaration merging useful in practice?
options: It lets you add properties to existing types, such as library types like Window
It converts interfaces into runtime classes
questions.explanation: Merging is how code augments existing declarations, for example adding a custom field to Window or to a framework's request type.
